Apply a Saved Binning Scheme to a Data Frame

bin_apply.Rd

Create a categorical column using the exact cutpoints and zero rule of a previously inspected diagnosis. No boundaries are recomputed.

Usage

bin_apply(data, scheme, name = NULL, variable = NULL,
  out_of_range = c("error", "NA"), warn = TRUE)

Arguments

data

A data frame containing the variable to categorize.

scheme

An unmodified bin_diagnosis returned by bin_diagnose(), or one selected element of bin_compare()$diagnoses.

name

New column name. Defaults to the receiving variable name followed by "_bin". Existing columns cannot be overwritten.

variable

Quoted source column name in the receiving data. Defaults to the variable name stored in the scheme. Must identify a plain numeric or integer column in the same units as the data used to define the scheme.

out_of_range

Default "error" stops if any finite value has no category under the saved scheme. Explicit "NA" retains such rows with missing categories. Boundaries are never extended and values are never clipped.

warn

Warn about unassigned observations. With FALSE, the audit report still records them. Invalid inputs and the default out-of-range error are unaffected.

Details

The output is an ordinary data frame, including when the input is a data-frame subclass. Original columns, row order, and row names are preserved, and the input object is not modified. The new column is an unordered factor, with all saved levels retained even when empty. Category identifiers follow the saved order. Intervals include their upper boundary; the first includes its lower boundary. A singleton category accepts only its exact saved value.

If zero separation was requested, exact zeros use the saved Zero category and only positive values enter the interval bins. If no Zero category existed when the scheme was created, a newly encountered zero is uncovered. No new category is invented. Negative values are uncovered under a separate-zero scheme even if custom cutpoints extend below zero. For an all-zero scheme, new positive values are uncovered. Custom cutpoints can cover new values beyond the original observed range, as long as those values satisfy the saved bounds and zero rule.

NA and NaN receive missing categories, as do positive and negative infinity. All rows remain present under the explicit "NA" out-of-range policy. The scheme's original assignment vector is not reused; each receiving value is assigned using the saved cutpoints. Percentage display options do not convert data units. The caller must supply values in compatible units.

An audit record is stored in attr(result, "binwise")[[name]]. It contains the receiving and original variable names, method, exact breaks, zero rule, category definition with closure indicators, out-of-range policy, and new-data summaries. summary counts total, finite, assigned, missing, infinite, and uncovered observations. counts gives each category's count and proportion of all finite receiving values, including uncovered finite values in the denominator. Proportions are NA if there are no finite values, and may sum to less than one if finite values are uncovered. excluded identifies unassigned row positions and their reasons. Counts are descriptive row counts.

Applying another scheme under a different column name preserves earlier audit records. These records describe the data at application time; later subsetting or editing does not recalculate them and may discard attributes. Save the whole object with saveRDS() to retain the factor and metadata. CSV export does not retain these attributes. The function does not choose a model or reference category; unordered factors avoid imposing ordered-factor polynomial contrasts.

Value

A data frame with the new factor column and a binwise audit attribute.

See also

bin_diagnose, bin_compare

Examples

training <- data.frame(x = c(0, 0, 1:8))
scheme <- bin_diagnose(training, "x", bins = 2,
                       separate_zero = TRUE, warn = FALSE)
binned <- bin_apply(training, scheme, name = "x_group")
table(binned$x_group, useNA = "ifany")
#> 
#> Zero   B1   B2 
#>    2    4    4 
attr(binned, "binwise")$x_group$definition
#>    bin lower upper left_closed right_closed singleton
#> 1 Zero   0.0   0.0        TRUE         TRUE      TRUE
#> 2   B1   1.0   4.5        TRUE         TRUE     FALSE
#> 3   B2   4.5   8.0       FALSE         TRUE     FALSE
new_data <- data.frame(x = c(0, 2, 6, 9, NA))
applied <- bin_apply(new_data, scheme, out_of_range = "NA", warn = FALSE)
attr(applied, "binwise")$x_bin$excluded
#>   row       reason
#> 1   4 out_of_range
#> 2   5      missing
